title: Sampling and Data: Census, Samples, Bias and Estimates
seo_title: Year 8 Sampling Worksheets: Census, Random Samples, Bias and Estimating Populations (Free, Answer Key)
standard_text: investigate techniques for data collection including census, sampling, experiment and observation, and explain the practicalities and implications of obtaining data through these techniques
meta_desc: Free Year 8 maths worksheets on sampling for the Australian Curriculum (AC9M8ST01): census, sample, experiment and observation, random and non-random samples, bias, estimating a population and comparing samples. 100 questions with an answer key.
key_big: A random sample gives everyone the same chance of being chosen.
key_sub: A sample can estimate a population: sample proportion × population size.
body_html:
How it works

A census collects data from every member of a population; a sample collects data from part of it. Data can also come from an experiment (changing something on purpose) or an observation (watching and recording). Data you collect is primary; data someone else collected is secondary.

A random sample gives everyone the same chance of being chosen. Non-random samples, such as asking your friends or whoever volunteers, are often biased. Larger random samples usually vary less.

To estimate a population, use the sample proportion: (number in sample ÷ sample size) × population.

Example

In a random sample of 50 students, 18 play an instrument. Estimate the number in a school of 800.

18 ÷ 50 = 0.36.

0.36 × 800.

Answer: 288 students

Example

Is asking 20 people at a dog park whether they like dogs a fair sample?

People at a dog park probably like dogs.

Answer: No, it is biased

Common mistakes

  • Thinking a large sample cannot be biased. A large sample from one group is still biased.
  • Choosing a convenient sample, such as your friends, instead of a random one.
  • Scaling the wrong way: if 9 out of 30 is the sample, multiply the population by 9/30, not 30/9.
  • Using the mean when an outlier makes it untypical. The median may be better.

faq.q: What is the difference between a census and a sample?
faq.a: A census collects data from every member of the population. A sample collects data from only part of it.
A sample is biased when some groups are more likely to be chosen than others, for example asking only your friends or only people at one place.

faq.q: How do I estimate a population from a sample?
faq.a: Find the fraction of the sample with the feature, then multiply it by the size of the population.

faq.q: Why do different samples give different results?
faq.a: Each random sample includes different people, so results vary. Larger samples usually vary less.

items.q: Every student at a school is asked how they travel to school.
items.e: Everyone in the population is asked: a census.

items.q: The Australian Bureau of Statistics collects information from every household in Australia every five years.
items.e: Every household is included: a census.

items.q: 100 voters out of 20 000 in a town are asked who they will vote for.
items.e: Only part of the population is asked: a sample.

items.q: A student counts how many cars pass the school gate between 8 am and 9 am.
items.e: Watching and recording what happens: an observation.

items.q: Half the tomato plants get a new fertiliser and half do not, and their growth is compared.
items.e: Changing one thing on purpose and measuring the effect: an experiment.

items.q: A student drops a ball from different heights and measures how high it bounces.
items.e: Changing the height on purpose and measuring: an experiment.

items.q: A scientist records which birds visit a feeder each morning for a month.
items.e: Recording what happens without changing it: an observation.

items.q: A company tests 50 light globes from a batch of 10 000 to see how long they last.
items.e: Only some globes are tested (testing all would destroy them): a sample.

items.q: Why does a factory test a sample of its matches rather than every match?
c: It is against the law to test them all
items.e: A test uses up the match, so testing every one would leave none to sell: testing destroys it.

items.q: What is the main advantage of a census over a sample?
c: It includes every member of the population
It needs fewer people to run it
items.e: A census includes everyone, so there is no sampling error.

items.q: What is the main advantage of a sample over a census?
items.e: A sample is quicker and cheaper than asking everyone.

items.q: Which is primary data?
c: Figures from the Bureau of Meteorology website
items.e: Primary data is collected by you; the others are secondary data.

items.q: Which is secondary data?
c: Times you record in a race
Rainfall records downloaded from the Bureau of Meteorology
Heights you measure in your class
A survey you give to your friends
items.e: Data someone else collected is secondary data.

items.q: A student wants to know if a new playground is used more at lunch than at recess. Which method is most suitable?
items.e: She can watch and count users at each break: observation.

items.q: Which question is best answered with an experiment?
c: What is the most popular sport at school?
How many birds visit a tree?
How many people live in Perth?
Does warm water dissolve sugar faster than cold water?
items.e: You can change the water temperature and measure the effect: an experiment.

items.q: A census of Australia is expensive. Why is it still carried out?
c: It is cheaper than a sample
Governments need accurate information about everyone to plan services
It is the only way to get data
items.e: Planning schools, hospitals and roads needs accurate information about everyone.

items.q: Which is NOT a practical problem with a census?
c: It only includes part of the population
items.e: A census includes everyone, so only part of the population is not one of its problems.

items.q: Why might observation data about animals be better than asking people about them?
c: People's memories and opinions can be inaccurate
items.e: Watching gives first-hand data, while people's memories and opinions can be inaccurate.

items.q: A researcher wants to know the average height of Year 8 students in Australia. What is most practical?
c: Measure a random sample of Year 8 students
items.e: A census would be huge; a random sample is practical and fair.

items.q: Which describes the population in a survey about the reading habits of students at Riverside High?
c: The students who answer the survey
items.e: The population is the whole group you want to know about: all students at Riverside High.

items.q: To find the most popular sport at school, Jack asks the members of the football team. Why is this sample biased?
c: Football players are likely to choose football
Sport is not a fair question
items.e: The people asked are not typical of the school: football players are likely to choose football.

items.q: To find how far people travel to work, a survey is given out at a train station. Why might it be biased?
c: It leaves out people who drive, walk or cycle
items.e: Only train users are asked, so people who drive, walk or cycle are left out.

items.q: Which is a random sample of 50 students from a school of 800?
c: Put all 800 names in a computer and select 50 at random
Ask the first 50 students through the gate
items.e: In a random sample every student has the same chance: select 50 at random from all 800 names.

items.q: A TV show asks viewers to text in their opinion. What kind of sample is this?
items.e: Only viewers who choose to reply are counted: self-selected.

items.q: Which is a systematic sample?
c: Choosing names out of a hat
Choosing every 10th name on the class roll
items.e: Choosing at regular intervals: systematic.

items.q: A survey about a new skate park is handed out at a skate shop. What is the problem?
c: Skaters are more likely to want a skate park
items.e: The sample is not representative: skaters are more likely to want a skate park.

items.q: Which question is biased?
c: What time would you like school to start?
How many hours of sleep do you get?
How do you travel to school?
Don't you agree that school should start later?
items.e: Don't you agree… pushes people towards one answer.

items.q: A sample of 1000 people is chosen only from Sydney to represent all Australians. What is the main problem?
c: It does not represent people from other places
items.e: A large sample can still be biased: it does not represent people from other places.

items.q: How can you reduce bias in a sample?
c: Choose people at random from the whole population
items.e: Random selection from the whole population gives everyone the same chance.

items.q: Why is a convenience sample (asking whoever is nearby) often not reliable?
c: The people nearby may not be typical of the population
items.e: Convenient people may share habits: they may not be typical.

items.q: Which sample is most likely to represent all students in a school of 1200?
c: A random sample of 100 students from the whole school
All 30 students in one Year 12 class
The first 100 students to reply to an email
items.e: A large random sample from the whole school is most representative.

items.q: A council wants residents' views on a new library. Which sample is least biased?
c: People who answer an online poll
A random selection of addresses from the electoral roll
items.e: Random addresses give every resident an equal chance.

items.q: Two classes each take a random sample of 20 students. Will they get exactly the same results?
c: No, because one sample must be biased
Only if they ask the same questions
items.e: Different random samples give different results: samples vary.

items.q: Which happens to the variation between random samples as the sample size increases?
c: It disappears for any sample over 10
items.e: Larger random samples usually vary less, so they are more reliable.

items.q: A stratified sample of 60 students is taken from a school with 300 boys and 300 girls. How many girls should be chosen?
items.e: Girls are half the school, so half the sample: 30.

items.q: A survey asks 'How much do you love our delicious new burger?' What is wrong with it?
items.e: The words lead people to a positive answer.

items.q: Which is non-random sampling?
c: Asking people who walk past at a shopping centre
Rolling a die to choose students
items.e: Choosing whoever walks past is non-random (convenience).

items.q: Ruby surveys 10 of her friends and finds that 9 like pineapple on pizza. She says 90% of Australians like it. What is the main problem?
c: Pizza is not a fair topic
She should have used a census
Her sample is small and not random
items.e: Ten friends are a small, non-random sample.

items.q: Online reviews of a restaurant are mostly very good or very bad. Why?
c: People with strong feelings are more likely to write a review
items.e: A self-selected sample attracts people with strong feelings.

items.q: Which sample size is most likely to give a reliable estimate, if all are chosen at random?
items.e: Larger random samples are more reliable: 400.

items.q: A random sample of 250 adults in a town of 20 000 finds that 115 want a new swimming pool. Estimate how many adults in the town want the pool.
A random sample of 250 adults in a town of 25 000 finds that 65 want a new swimming pool. Estimate how many adults in the town want the pool.
A random sample of 500 adults in a town of 40 000 finds that 100 want a new swimming pool. Estimate how many adults in the town want the pool.
In a random sample, 20% of the trees in a forest have a disease. The forest has 500 trees. Estimate how many have the disease.
A random sample of 250 adults in a town of 8000 finds that 75 want a new swimming pool. Estimate how many adults in the town want the pool.
In a random sample of 100 students from a school of 800, 41 walk to school. Estimate how many students in the whole school walk to school.
items.e: 41 out of 100 is 0.41 of the sample. 0.41 × 800 = 328.

items.q: In a random sample of 50 students from a school of 1500, 42 have a pet dog. Estimate how many students in the whole school have a pet dog.
items.e: 42 out of 50 is 0.84 of the sample. 0.84 × 1500 = 1260.

items.q: In a random sample of 100 students from a school of 1500, 83 play a musical instrument. Estimate how many students in the whole school play a musical instrument.
items.e: 83 out of 100 is 0.83 of the sample. 0.83 × 1500 = 1245.

items.q: In a random sample, 8% of the trees in a forest have a disease. The forest has 3000 trees. Estimate how many have the disease.
A random sample of 250 adults in a town of 5000 finds that 95 want a new swimming pool. Estimate how many adults in the town want the pool.
In a random sample of 100 students from a school of 600, 71 walk to school. Estimate how many students in the whole school walk to school.
items.e: 71 out of 100 is 0.71 of the sample. 0.71 × 600 = 426.

items.q: A random sample of 200 adults in a town of 20 000 finds that 45 want a new swimming pool. Estimate how many adults in the town want the pool.
In a random sample of 100 students from a school of 600, 52 catch the bus. Estimate how many students in the whole school catch the bus.
items.e: 52 out of 100 is 0.52 of the sample. 0.52 × 600 = 312.

items.q: A random sample of 200 adults in a town of 8000 finds that 45 want a new swimming pool. Estimate how many adults in the town want the pool.
Rangers catch 30 fish in a lake, tag them and release them. Later they catch 40 fish and 5 are tagged. Estimate the number of fish in the lake.
items.e: 5 out of 40 caught are tagged, so the 30 tagged fish are about 5/40 of the lake. 30 × 40 ÷ 5 = 240.

items.q: In a random sample, 45% of the trees in a forest have a disease. The forest has 3000 trees. Estimate how many have the disease.
A random sample of 250 adults in a town of 20 000 finds that 85 want a new swimming pool. Estimate how many adults in the town want the pool.
In a random sample of 50 students from a school of 900, 34 play a musical instrument. Estimate how many students in the whole school play a musical instrument.
items.e: 34 out of 50 is 0.68 of the sample. 0.68 × 900 = 612.

items.q: In a random sample of 50 students from a school of 800, 40 have a pet dog. Estimate how many students in the whole school have a pet dog.
items.e: 40 out of 50 is 0.8 of the sample. 0.8 × 800 = 640.

items.q: A random sample of 200 adults in a town of 5000 finds that 85 want a new swimming pool. Estimate how many adults in the town want the pool.
A sample shows the books read last term by 5 students: 11, 8, 16, 11, 19. What is the median?
items.e: In order: 8, 11, 11, 16, 19. The middle value is 11.

items.q: A sample shows the goals scored by a netball team in 7 games: 3, 17, 5, 3, 15, 3, 11. What is the median?
items.e: In order: 3, 3, 3, 5, 11, 15, 17. The middle value is 5.

items.q: A sample shows the books read last term by 5 students: 15, 3, 19, 17, 3. What is the mean?
A sample shows the text messages sent in a day by 7 students: 5, 16, 14, 12, 20, 12, 10. What is the range?
items.e: Range = largest − smallest = 20 − 5 = 15.

items.q: A sample shows the books read last term by 7 students: 7, 13, 20, 16, 9, 3, 15. What is the median?
items.e: In order: 3, 7, 9, 13, 15, 16, 20. The middle value is 13.

items.q: A sample shows the goals scored by a netball team in 7 games: 18, 2, 7, 9, 18, 20, 20. What is the range?
items.e: Range = largest − smallest = 20 − 2 = 18.

items.q: A sample shows the books read last term by 5 students: 17, 4, 2, 2, 3. What is the median?
items.e: In order: 2, 2, 3, 4, 17. The middle value is 3.

items.q: A sample shows the goals scored by a netball team in 6 games: 9, 7, 3, 10, 11, 18. What is the median?
items.e: In order: 3, 7, 9, 10, 11, 18. The middle two values average to 9.5.

items.q: A sample shows the goals scored by a netball team in 6 games: 14, 8, 4, 6, 12, 3. What is the range?
items.e: Range = largest − smallest = 14 − 3 = 11.

items.q: A sample shows the books read last term by 7 students: 13, 9, 14, 17, 6, 12, 4. What is the median?
items.e: In order: 4, 6, 9, 12, 13, 14, 17. The middle value is 12.

items.q: A sample shows the goals scored by a netball team in 6 games: 5, 3, 11, 20, 12, 12. What is the median?
items.e: In order: 3, 5, 11, 12, 12, 20. The middle two values average to 11.5.

items.q: A sample shows the goals scored by a netball team in 6 games: 3, 14, 3, 6, 12, 7. What is the mean?
A sample shows the goals scored by a netball team in 7 games: 3, 4, 19, 7, 19, 12, 10. What is the range?
items.e: Range = largest − smallest = 19 − 3 = 16.

items.q: A sample shows the goals scored by a netball team in 7 games: 2, 15, 16, 20, 6, 2, 7. What is the median?
items.e: In order: 2, 2, 6, 7, 15, 16, 20. The middle value is 7.

items.q: A sample shows the text messages sent in a day by 5 students: 8, 18, 13, 10, 14. What is the median?
items.e: In order: 8, 10, 13, 14, 18. The middle value is 13.

items.q: A sample shows the text messages sent in a day by 6 students: 18, 5, 5, 8, 16, 8. What is the mean?
A sample shows the books read last term by 5 students: 20, 2, 3, 14, 9. What is the median?
items.e: In order: 2, 3, 9, 14, 20. The middle value is 9.

items.q: A sample shows the books read last term by 7 students: 2, 10, 15, 5, 20, 20, 20. What is the median?
items.e: In order: 2, 5, 10, 15, 20, 20, 20. The middle value is 15.

items.q: A sample shows the books read last term by 5 students: 10, 12, 20, 11, 18. What is the range?
items.e: Range = largest − smallest = 20 − 10 = 10.

items.q: A sample shows the books read last term by 6 students: 19, 19, 6, 4, 6, 4. What is the range?
items.e: Range = largest − smallest = 19 − 4 = 15.

items.q: Sample A of 20 students has a mean height of 158 cm. Sample B of 200 students has a mean of 156 cm. Which is likely to be closer to the mean of the whole year group?
items.e: Larger random samples are usually more reliable: Sample B.

items.q: Five random samples of 10 students give the proportion who walk to school as 0.3, 0.5, 0.2, 0.4 and 0.6. What is the mean of these proportions?
In the five samples above, what is the range of the proportions?
If the samples above had 100 students each instead of 10, what would you expect?
items.e: Larger samples usually vary less.

items.q: A sample's data is 3, 4, 4, 5, 5, 6, 48. Which is the best measure of a typical value?
c: The mean, because it uses every value
The mode, because 4 and 5 both appear twice
The median, because 48 is an outlier
items.e: One outlier pulls the mean up to 10.7. The median (5) is more typical.

items.q: Two samples of Year 8 test scores have the same mean of 65. Sample A has a range of 20 and Sample B has a range of 60. What does this tell you?
c: Sample B's scores are more spread out
items.e: A larger range means the scores are more spread out.

items.q: A sample of 50 Year 8 students finds 12 are left-handed. What percentage is this?
A sample of 40 from School A finds 10 cycle to school. A sample of 60 from School B finds 12 cycle. Which school's sample has the greater proportion of cyclists?
c: You cannot compare different sample sizes

items.q: Which data is categorical?
items.e: Favourite colour is a category, not a number.

items.q: Which data is continuous numerical?
items.e: Time can take any value in a range: continuous.

items.q: Which data is discrete numerical?
items.e: You count siblings in whole numbers: discrete.

items.q: The ages of a random sample of people at a beach are mostly 15 to 30, with a few older people. How would you describe the distribution?
c: Skewed, with a tail of older ages
items.e: Most values are low with a few high ones: skewed, with a tail of older ages.

items.q: A random sample of 80 apples from an orchard has 6 bruised apples. The orchard has 4000 apples. Estimate the number of bruised apples.
Which statement about samples is TRUE?
c: A census is a type of sample
A random sample always matches the population exactly
A biased sample is fine if it is large
A random sample can still give a result that differs from the population
items.e: Random samples vary, so a sample can differ from the population.

items.q: A survey of 30 people at a gym finds they exercise 6 hours a week on average. Why should this not be used for all adults?
c: Gym members probably exercise more than most adults
items.e: The sample is biased: gym members probably exercise more.

items.q: Which graph best shows how a sample of heights is distributed?
c: A line graph of height against date
items.e: A histogram or dot plot shows the shape and spread of numerical data.

items.q: The median number of hours of screen time in a sample is 3. What does this mean?
c: Half the sample had 3 hours or less
The average of the highest and lowest is 3
items.e: The median is the middle value, so half the sample had 3 hours or less.

items.q: A sample of 25 students has a mean of 12 books read. The total for the sample is…
items.e: Total = mean × number = 12 × 25 = 300.

items.q: In a sample, the mean is much larger than the median. What does this suggest?
c: There are some very large values
There are some very small values
items.e: A few very large values pull the mean up: there are some very large values.

items.q: Why do researchers often take several random samples instead of one?
c: Because one sample is always wrong
To see how much the results vary
items.e: Several samples show how much results vary, which helps judge reliability.
